article_sections.section: # PathRAG: Pruning Graph-based Retrieval Augmented Generation with Relational Paths
section_highlights: PathRAG: Pruning Graph-based Retrieval Augmented Generation with Relational Paths
Authors: Boyu Chen, Zirui Guo, Zidan Yang, Yuluo Chen, Junze Chen, Zhenghao Liu, Chuan Shi, Cheng Yang
article_sections.section_keywords: PathRAG, Graph-based Retrieval, Augmented Generation, Relational Paths

section_highlights: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) improves response quality of large language models (LLMs) by retrieving knowledge from external databases.
Graph-based RAG methods have limitations due to redundancy of retrieved information, not insufficiency.
PathRAG reduces redundant information with flow-based pruning and guides LLMs to generate more logical and coherent responses with path-based prompting.
PathRAG consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across six datasets and five evaluation dimensions.
The code for PathRAG is available at https://github.com/BUPT-GAMMA/PathRAG
article_sections.section_keywords: Retrieval-augmented generation, Graph-based RAG, PathRAG, Large Language Models, Knowledge Retrieval

section_highlights: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances large language models (LLMs) by accessing external databases for up-to-date knowledge.
Graph-based RAG organizes textual information into an indexing graph to capture dependencies and relationships across texts.
PathRAG proposes a key path retrieval method to alleviate noise and reduce token consumption in RAG.
PathRAG outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across six datasets and five evaluation dimensions.
The limitations of current graph-based RAG methods lie in the redundancy of retrieved information and the use of a flat structure.
article_sections.section_keywords: Retrieval-Augmented Generation, Large Language Models, Graph-Based RAG, PathRAG, Key Path Retrieval, Noise Reduction, Token Consumption

section_highlights: Text-based RAG improves text quality and mitigates hallucination effects by leveraging external databases.
Text-based RAG can be broadly classified into two categories: sparse vector retrieval and dense vector retrieval.
Dense vector retrieval addresses issues like lexical mismatches and synonyms by encoding query terms and text into vector embeddings.
KG-RAG retrieves information from knowledge graphs, enabling LLMs to retrieve information of relevant entities and their relationships.
Graph-based RAG organizes text databases as text-associated graphs, focusing on global-level questions that need information from multiple segments across a database.
GraphRAG and LightRAG are two graph-based RAG methods that accelerate the retrieval process and handle global-level tasks effectively.
article_sections.section_keywords: text-based RAG, dense vector retrieval, KG-RAG, graph-based RAG, retrieval-augmented generation

section_highlights: Graph-based RAG system workflow is introduced and formalized.
Indexing graph is constructed from text database with entities and interrelations identified by LLMs.
Graph-oriented retriever extracts relevant nodes and edges in the indexing graph.
Augmented generation with retrieval results is denoted as $mathcal{A}(q, mathcal{G})$.
Designing an effective graph-oriented retriever and prompt template is the primary focus of this paper.
article_sections.section_keywords: graph-based RAG, indexing graph, graph-oriented retriever, LLMs, augmented generation

section_highlights: A novel graph-based RAG framework, PathRAG, is proposed for information retrieval.
The framework operates in three stages: node retrieval, path retrieval, and answer generation.
Node retrieval uses LLMs to extract keywords from the input query and retrieve related nodes from the indexing graph.
Path retrieval employs a flow-based pruning algorithm to extract key paths between retrieved nodes.
Answer generation prioritizes paths based on reliability and positions them to align with LLMs' performance patterns.
The framework addresses the 'lost in the middle' issue in long-context scenarios by positioning critical information at the template's ends.
article_sections.section_keywords: Graph-based RAG framework, PathRAG, node retrieval, path retrieval, answer generation, LLMs, information retrieval, flow-based pruning algorithm, reliability-based prioritization, long-context scenarios

section_highlights: PathRAG consistently outperforms the baselines across all evaluation dimensions and datasets.
PathRAG shows an average win rate of 60.88% in Comprehensiveness, 62.75% in Diversity, 59.78% in Logicality, 60.47% in Relevance, and 59.93% in Coherence.
The proposed path-based retrieval contributes to better performance across multiple aspects of the generated responses.
PathRAG reduces 16% token cost with much better performance, and the corresponding monetary cost is only $0.002.
PathRAG-lt reduces 44% tokens while maintaining comparable performance to LightRAG.

section_highlights: The work focuses on retrieving information from an indexing graph for answering questions.
The indexing graph construction process is not explored for fair comparison with previous methods.
PathRAG involves no deep neural networks or parameter training for simplicity.
The evaluation metrics are relative rather than absolute.
Future work includes collecting more datasets and designing new metrics for graph-based RAG.

section_highlights: Six datasets are used in the experiments, covering various domains.
Datasets include agriculture, legal, history, CS, biology, and mix.
Each dataset provides detailed information on its respective domain.
The datasets cover a wide range of topics, including practices, events, and figures.
The CS dataset focuses on machine learning and big data applications.

section_highlights: NaiveRAG uses text embeddings for efficient and direct access to answers.
HyDE shares a similar storage framework with NaiveRAG but uses an LLM to generate a hypothetical document for retrieval.
GraphRAG is a graph-based RAG that uses an LLM to extract entities and relationships from text, with community detection for summarization.
LightRAG is a graph-based RAG that employs a dual-level retrieval framework for more precise searches and reduced token and time consumption.
LLM evaluates RAG responses based on five dimensions: Comprehensiveness, Diversity, Logicality, Relevance, and Coherence.
Two path ordering methods: Random and Hop-first ordering are used to select K paths.
Two prompt formats: Flat organization and structured organization are used to arrange retrieved paths.
The goal of path ordering is to enhance memory retention by placing the most important paths at the end of the prompt.
The LLM assesses the relevance of paths based on the number of hops, with fewer hops indicating more direct relevance.
